out: The Palestinian Authority officially joined the International Criminal Court on Wednesday, granting the court jurisdiction over alleged crimes in Palestinian territories. The formal accession at The Hague marks a significant step toward accountability, though Israel and the United States oppose the move, arguing it undermines peace efforts.

A stray dog in Washington State survived a harrowing sequence of being hit by a car, struck with a hammer, and buried alive, only to dig her way to a farm four days later. Now named Theia, the dog is recovering from severe injuries including a dislocated jaw and sinus cavity, with her rescuer aiming to find her a permanent home. Donations have already surpassed $10,000 to cover her extensive medical needs, inspiring comparisons to other animals like a Florida cat that also cheated death after being buried.

Mohammad Javad Zarif, Iran's newly appointed foreign minister, was welcomed as a hero upon his return to Tehran, marking a significant step in nuclear negotiations with the U.S. and potentially ending sanctions. Despite his high-profile role, much about Zarif remains obscure, including a bizarre discrepancy in his official birth date—listed as either 1959, 1960, or 1961—and his academic background, having earned three degrees from U.S. universities during the height of the Iranian Revolution. Five Americans exposed to Ebola in Sierra Leone were released from an Omaha hospital after three weeks of monitoring, though one remains locally due to a heart issue. The group, who are clinicians with Partners in Health, had contact with a colleague currently being treated at NIH Bethesda, as the CDC expects the last of 17 monitored patients to be released by Thursday.

A Duke student was identified and admitted to hanging a noose from a tree near the student union. The university stated the student is no longer on campus and will face conduct review, while officials continue to investigate if others were involved. Students and faculty marched in protest, chanting "We are not afraid. We stand together" following the incident.

Trey Moses, a star basketball player at Eastern High School, asked Ellie Meredith, a freshman with Down syndrome, to be his prom date instead of his girlfriend, sparking a viral social media moment. The gesture, which included a "prom-posal" set to a Taylor Swift reference and parental approval, was celebrated by Ellie's mother as a meaningful inclusion for her daughter, who had previously struggled with friendships. Amnesty International alleges governments are using the threat of terrorism to advance executions, noting a marked increase in death sentences globally while executions worldwide dropped by 22%. The report highlights Pakistan and China as examples of this trend, though it notes positive developments such as reduced executions in the Middle East and Sub-Saharan Africa.

Andrew Getty, an heir to the Getty oil fortune, died at age 47 from natural causes, according to the Los Angeles Police Department. The death was ruled as natural, with the coroner noting that Getty had "several health issues" and had been diagnosed with a serious medical condition in 2013. His parents confirmed his death and requested privacy as the family mourned his loss.

Filipinos are being warned to prepare for flash floods and landslides as tropical storm Maysak approaches, having recently peaked as a super typhoon with 150 mph winds. Authorities have issued preemptive evacuations and travel restrictions, with the storm expected to make landfall in Isabela province Sunday morning before exiting the Philippines by Monday.

Bob Barker, 91, returned to "The Price Is Right" for the first time in eight years to host the "Lucky Seven" game, proving he still "didn't seem to miss a beat" before passing the reins to Drew Carey. The appearance marked a rare return for the longtime host, who led the show for 35 years before retiring in 2007.

A 19-year-old man was charged with terror offenses after being arrested upon his return to Britain from Turkey. Yahya Rashid was detained at Luton airport and faces charges related to preparing for and assisting in acts of terrorism between November and March. He is due to appear in court on Wednesday.

Paul Walker's death during the production of "Furious 7" prompted a poignant tribute, with the film's release serving as a bittersweet celebration of his life. Producers utilized his brothers as body doubles and rewrote the script to complete the film without killing off his character, Brian O'Connor. At the premiere, co-star Vin Diesel delivered a tearful speech emphasizing the film's emotional impact, stating it forces audiences to "appreciate everyone you love."

New research suggests Anne Frank and her sister Margot likely died in February 1945, at least a month earlier than previously believed. Researchers re-examined Red Cross archives and survivor testimonies, concluding the sisters perished from a typhus outbreak at Bergen-Belsen just weeks before the camp's liberation. Despite the revised timeline, Anne's diary remains a powerful testament, with friends recalling her unshakable belief that she would survive.

A year after Bloomberg reported Mike Pence as a Koch-backed contender for the 2016 presidency, the Indiana governor has faced intense backlash for signing a religious freedom law seen as discriminatory against LGBTQ individuals. The controversy has energued the GOP's conservative base and drawn Pence and other potential candidates further to the right, transforming LGBTQ rights into a central issue for the 2016 primary race rather than a peripheral topic.

Performing the "Star-Spangled Banner" is a high-risk endeavor where artists can swing from hero to disgrace; Vince Neil’s recent flub and Roseanne Barr’s historical booing illustrate the volatile reception, while legends like Whitney Houston and Jimi Hendrix set the gold and silver standards respectively. Conversely, Michael Bolton’s 2003 performance was criticized for lyrical inaccuracies, proving that even "overly wrought" renditions can draw scorn if the words are botched.

Walmart's opposition to religious freedom laws in Arkansas and other states highlights a growing corporate stance against discrimination, warning that such legislation would open the door to anti-LGBTQ customer treatment. Former Minnesota Gov. Tim Pawlenty argues the GOP must evolve to support "modidne income workers" and prohibit discrimination, signaling a shift in Republican Party priorities. Ultimately, Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson vetoed the bill after Walmart's pressure, illustrating how major retailers are becoming bellwethers for shifting public opinion on hot-button political issues that divide conservatives and liberals.

In May 2014, China held a mass sentencing in Xinjiang where 55 people were jailed and three were executed, part of a government campaign against unrest. Amnesty International's report highlights a global trend of governments increasingly resorting to the death penalty in misguided attempts to combat terrorism and crime, despite a lack of evidence that it deters crime more effectively than imprisonment.

The French prosecutor leading the investigation into the Germanwings Flight 9525 crash denied knowledge of any onboard video footage, despite claims from two magazines that they recovered a cell phone video from the wreckage. Paris Match and Bild reported the video showed the final seconds of the flight, including the pilot attempting to open the cockpit door and passengers screaming, though they did not publish the clip. An official with the BEA accident investigation agency and a French Gendarmerie spokesman both stated they were not aware of such video evidence, noting that cell phones found at the site had not yet been analyzed.

Rev. Robert H. Schuller, the 88-year-old televangelist and founder of the "Hour of Power" ministry, died Thursday. He had been battling esophageal cancer since 2013 and was remembered for pioneering televised religious programming and building the Crystal Cathedral megachurch. His legacy is defined by his "possibility thinking" message and his transition from drive-in theater preaching to global television broadcasts.

Michele Bachmann compared President Obama to Andreas Lubitz, the co-pilot who crashed Germanwings Flight 9525, arguing that the Iran nuclear deal puts the U.S. in danger. She suggested Obama is "deliberately flying the nation into the rocks," drawing parallels to the Germanwings disaster. Bachmann's controversial remarks have drawn sharp criticism, with some accusing her of seeking attention through inflammatory comparisons as nuclear negotiations approach a deadline.

The second mate of the Houston Express rescued Louis Jordan, a 37-year-old man who had survived 66 days adrift at sea after his 35-foot sailboat capsized twice off the coast of South Carolina. Despite facing storms, shark-infested waters, and the challenge of collecting fresh water, Jordan was found in surprisingly good condition, credibly creded by his father and Coast Guard officials after being spotted signaling for help from his capsized vessel.

The United States and its P5+1 partners reached a framework agreement with Iran that effectively blocks Iran from building a nuclear weapon by reducing its uranium stockpile and centrifuge count, though the deal faces significant political opposition in the U.S. Congress. The agreement is designed to prevent a covert Iranian nuclear arsenal through rigorous inspections, and its rejection by Congress could unravel sanctions and threaten transatlantic alliances.

The California drought, now in its fourth year, threatens national food supplies as the state produces a significant portion of the U.S. vegetables and fruits. This has already driven up prices for specific items like berries and broccoli in 2014, and economists project further increases of 2.5% to 3.5% for fresh fruit and vegetables this year, though a strong dollar and lower oil prices may partially offset these costs. The FBI charged a Philadelphia woman, Keonna Thomas, with attempting to travel overseas to join ISIS, making her one of three women arrested this week on terror charges. Two New York women were also arrested for allegedly planning to build an explosive device for attacks in the United States. Authorities cited social media messages from August 2013 showing Thomas's intent to join the fight, and she purchased an electronic visa to Turkey, known as a gateway to Syria.

Since Iran's 1979 Islamic Revolution, women have been barred from most men's sports events, but Deputy Sports Minister Abdolhamid Ahmadi announced a plan to allow "women and families" to enter stadiums next year, starting with indoor events. While the restrictions won't change for all matches due to cultural resistance, the move marks a significant shift from the long-standing ban that previously prevented Iranian women from attending soccer and other men's games. Online activity has emerged as the primary alternative to traditional mainstream media, particularly in authoritarian countries where access to print and broadcast is restricted. While the low cost of posting online is liberating, the lack of access to traditional media is the main driver pushing dissident voices online, though this comes with significant legal and physical risks. The article highlights cases in Singapore and Malaysia where bloggers face arrest, heavy financial penalties, and imprisonment for criticizing the government or addressing sensitive religious and political issues.

Avril Lavigne revealed she was bedridden for five months after contracting Lyme disease, which she believes she contracted from a tick bite last spring. The singer described feeling unable to breathe, talk, or move, and spent her recovery period at home with her husband and mother providing care. Now declaring herself "80 percent better," Lavigne is releasing new music to support the 2015 Special Olympics and says the illness was a "wake-up call" that has given her a fresh perspective on life.

This week's top videos feature a tour of Mike Tyson's former Ohio mansion, now being converted into a church; the world's tallest and fastest roller coaster at Carowinds; a CNN exclusive interview with Bikram Choudhury's former students alleging sexual assault; and a shepherd's eyewitness account of the Germanwings Flight 9525 crash.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu criticized the Iran nuclear deal as a "bad deal," arguing that standing firm and increasing pressure would yield a better agreement. While President Obama and Democrats support the framework, which limits Iran's centrifuges and uranium enrichment, Republicans and Netanyahu contend it grants too much flexibility and fails to dismantle Iran's nuclear infrastructure. Democratic leaders urge restraint, warning that opposition undermines a historic opportunity to prevent an Iranian bomb.

Memories Pizza in Walkerton, Indiana, became the center of a national debate after owners refused to cater a same-sex wedding due to religious beliefs, sparking both boycotts and support. The restaurant faced intense backlash, including death threats and a vandalism attempt, but supporters raised over $842,000 via GoFundMe, arguing the backlash represented intolerance rather than a defense of religious freedom.

Police in Malegaon are requiring identity cards for cattle following a statewide ban on beef, manduring residents to submit mugshots and details of their animals to solve slaughter cases. The move comes after a recent cow slaughter case and the new Maharashtra Animal Preservation Bill, which includes strict penalties and bans on bull slaughter, prompting beef traders to strike and challenge the restrictions in court.

Three people were stranded at sea for extended periods, relying on ingenuity to survive. Louis Jordan was rescued after months adrift, surviving by rationating water and catching fish with improvised tools. Jose Salvador Alvarenga was found on a remote atoll over a year after departing Mexico, having lost his companion and endured extreme hardship.

The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has resumed operations after a two-year shutdown, with the first particle beams successfully circulating the 17-mile ring on Sunday. Scientists at CERN hope the restart will help uncover the origins of mass, dark matter, and the fundamental forces of the universe by recreating conditions moments after the Big Bang. While the machine is in "great shape," researchers emphasize that the most significant phase of the experiment is still to come when beam energies are increased to new record levels.

FBI agents and task force officers pursued 36-year-old Kevone Charleston into a CVS pharmacy in Forsyth County, Georgia, where he was shot and captured after crashing into multiple government vehicles and injuring two agents. The suspect, wanted for 32 commercial robberies since November 2013, was found to have an "MO involving armed confrontations," and though the agents were released from the hospital, Emmett stated, "they are fine."

A nearly five-minute total lunar eclipse will occur this morning, marking the shortest such event of the century. Visible across western North America and parts of South America, India, and Russia, the " blood moon" phenomenon happens as the Earth passes between the sun and moon, filtering sunlight to create a reddish hue. While the total phase is brief, a partial eclipse will be visible nationally, though sunrise will cut the show short on the East Coast.

Al-Shabaab claimed responsibility for a deadly attack on Garissa University College in eastern Kenya, highlighting the deteriorating security situation in East Africa. The group, which split from Unity of Islam in 2003 and pledged allegiance to al-Qaeda in 2012, has escalated cross-border raids, predominantly targeting Christians, following the 2013 Westgate Shopping Centre massacre. Ethiopia's military response and regional instability have fueled the group's expansion, making the Garissa attack a clear indicator of the ongoing regional context of instability.

Easter is a cornerstone Christian event celebrating Christ's Resurrection, but its date shifts each spring based on the lunisolar calendar rather than a fixed date. While Western Christians celebrated Easter this Sunday, Eastern Orthodox Christians will mark it next week due to differing calendars. The holiday's timing is linked to the " blood moon" and the First Sunday after the Paschal full moon, connecting the celebration to cosmic events and the Church of the Holy Sepulcher in Jerusalem.

The NCAA is arguing it has no legal responsibility to ensure student-athletes receive a legitimate education, even after acknowledging its commitment to academics. This stance came in response to a lawsuit by former UNC athletes who claimed they were funneled into fraudulent classes to remain eligible to play sports. The organization likened its role to professional associations like the American Bar or Medical Association, asserting it is not liable for academic integrity at member schools.

A Connecticut judge denied a motion to release a 17-year-old girl from state custody, keeping her in temporary care despite her being in remission from Hodgkin lymphoma. The ruling came after her attorneys argued she was no longer at imminent risk of harm and could return to her mother, but the court maintained that the Department of Children and Families retain custody. While her lawyer noted she is feeling well and treatment is nearly complete, the state agency continues to view her as a "flight" and has not withdrawn its position for the custody order.

Mark Ronson's "Uptown Funk!" featuring Bruno Mars has reached its 13th week at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, making it the longest-leading song of the 2010s decade. The track has also joined an elite group of songs to top the chart for at least 13 weeks, solidifying its status as one of the most successful hits in the Hot 100's history.

Antica recorded a temperature of 63.5°F on March 24, potentially the highest ever recorded on the continent. The reading, taken at Argentina's Esperanza Base, is currently under review by a World Meteorological Organization committee of experts to verify the measurement. Researchers are closely monitoring the event as evidence of global warming.

Indiana's new Religious Freedom Restoration Act has sparked controversy by potentially using faith as a pretext to discriminate against gay people, joining a growing trend of state laws that have expanded since the 1993 federal act. However, legal experts note that claims under these laws are "exceedingly rare" and have mostly benefited religious minorities rather than Christian denominations, casting doubt on whether they provide meaningful protections. Robert Lewis Burns Jr., the original drummer for Lynyrd Skynyrd, died Friday night in a car crash in Georgia at age 64. The accident occurred when his car hit a mailbox and a tree, and he was pronounced dead at the scene. Burns, who left the band in 1975, was not involved in the 1977 plane crash that killed other members, and is survived by the band's only remaining original member, Gary Rossington.

The man accused of stabbing U.S. Ambassador Mark Lippert in Seoul last month has been charged with attempted murder and other related offenses. Kim Ki-Jong, who opposed the joint South Korean-U.S. military drills, was arrested after slashing the ambassador in the face and arm, requiring 80 stitches. South Korean authorities are investigating a possible connection between the attacker's past visits to North Korea and the attack.

A former banker, Rurik Jutting, was charged with two counts of murder after two women were found dead in a Hong Kong apartment. One victim, Seneng Mujiasih, was a domestic worker who had overstayed her visa, while the other, Sumarti Ningsih, was an Indonesian tourist who had been killed days earlier. The case has sparked outrage among fellow domestic workers and the victims' families, who are calling for justice as the court adjourns until May.

Thai Smile, a subsidiary of Thai Airways, has unveiled a new Airbus A320 featuring characters from "Adventure Time," including Jake, Finn, and Princess Bubblegum. The plane's interior is fully themed with character-adorn amenities like overhead bins and airsickness bags. The inaugural flight from Bangkok to Phuket is set to depart on April 4th.

Chelsea Manning, the imprisoned former Army intelligence analyst, has joined Twitter to communicate with the public, using a voice phone to dictate her posts due to a lack of internet access in prison. The 35-year prisoner, who was convicted of leaking classified documents, stated she wants the account to foster conversation rather be a one-way street. Manning, who is serving her sentence at Fort Leavenworth, was formally granted the name Chelsea Elizabeth Manning last year after undergoing hormone therapy for gender dysphoria.

President Obama tied his political legacy to securing a nuclear deal with Iran, viewing it as a defining achievement of his administration. However, the negotiation process has been weakened by political considerations, leaving the U.S. appearing eager while Iran's economy suffers, and resulting in a framework agreement that many doubt can prevent Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons. The deal's future remains uncertain, as its collapse could define Obama's foreign policy legacy, potentially emboldening regional rivals like Saudi Arabia to pursue their own nuclear capabilities.

"Furious 7" is poised to launch with $135-$138 million domestically, marking the biggest opening since fall 2013 and the largest of 2015 to date. The film, which serves as a send-off for the late Paul Walker, is also tracking for a massive global debut potentially crossing $300 million by Easter Sunday. Universal has expanded the release to a record 4,003 theaters domestically and over 10,500 screens internationally to accommodate the high demand.

Deion Sanders publicly scarified his son, Deion Sanders Jr., on Twitter for referring to "hood doughnuts," reminding him he has a trust fund, a condo, and his own clothing line. The elder Sanders emphasized his son's privileged status by labeling him a "Huxtable" and telling him to stop with the "hood stuff." Junior, a wide receiver at SMU and aspiring entrepreneur, seemingly took the public dressing in stride by retweet ing his father's comments.

A Columbia Journalism School review found Rolling Stone committed an "institutional failure" in its flawed UVA gang rape article, citing failures in reporting, editing, and fact-checking. The magazine apologized to readers and those damaged, including the Phi Kappa Psi fraternity. While the fraternity and UVA face complex legal hurdles, the report's findings likely help establish the "intent" needed for a defamation lawsuit, though strict rules on who can sue and the high bar for proving falsity remain significant obstacles.

Shibuya ward in Tokyo has passed an ordinance allowing same-sex couples to receive "partnership certificates," granting them limited rights such as hospital visitation and co-signing leases. While the certificates are not legally binding and fall short of full marriage rights, proponents view the move as a significant first step toward marriage equality in a socially conservative Japan. Neighboring districts are considering similar measures, but activists stress that a national law is ultimately required to achieve full equal rights.

Blue Bell has temporarily closed its Broken Arrow, Oklahoma plant after listeria was found in ice cream from that facility. The CDC warns consumers not to eat specific 3-ounce servings marked with codes O, P, Q, R, S, or T, while other Blue Bell products remain safe. This action is part of an ongoing investigation into a listeria outbreak linked to the company's ice cream, which has resulted in multiple recalls and tragic outcomes including hospitalizations and deaths.

In a recent Diet session, former wrestler Antonio Inoki asked if Japan's Air Self-Defense Force had ever scrambled jets to intercept extraterrestrial threats. Defense Minister Gen Nakatani firmly responded that the force had never encountered a UFO believed to come from outer space, noting they typically identify birds or non-aircraft objects instead. While Inoki claimed a personal UFO sighting and pushed for alien research, the exchange highlighted a long-standing political curiosity about the legal ramifications of a potential space invasion.

Residents of central Sanaa are enduring the harsh reality of strategic bombing in their neighborhoods, as airstrikes have shattered windows, killed hundreds, and left 16 million without electricity. President Hadi has dismissed his army chief, while the International Committee of the Red Cross has urgently called for a humanitarian ceasefire to prevent further deaths, though Saudi Arabia has pledged to allow aid deliveries into the war-torn country.

David Lynch has confirmed he will no longer direct the "Twin Peaks" revival, citing financial disputes with the network. The acclaimed director stated he felt the show was not being funded "the way it needed to be done," and he personally notified the cast of his departure. Showtime has expressed sadness over the decision but remains hopeful the series can return with both of its creators at the helm.

University of Kentucky guard Andrew Harrison apologized for using a racial slur under his breath after the team's loss to Wisconsin, stating he meant no disrespect to Badgers star Frank Kaminsky. Kaminsky said he was "over it" after the two spoke, and Harrison wished him well before the national championship game.

The FBI confirmed that Zulkifli bin Hir, known as Marwan, was killed in a disastrous January raid in the Philippines. The operation resulted in the deaths of 44 Philippine police officers and 19 MILF fighters, shattering a three-year ceasefire. The FBI has since removed Marwan from its "Most Wanted Terrorists" list following forensic confirmation of his death.

A Delaware family fell ill after staying at a luxury villa in the U.S. Virgin Islands, with the EPA reporting the presence of methyl bromide—a restricted indoor pesticide. Authorities are investigating whether the family was sickened following a fumigation on March 18, while Terminix, the licensed pest control company, is cooperating with the ongoing criminal and regulatory probe.

Chris Rock documented three traffic stops in seven weeks, highlighting the phenomenon of "driving while black" and the disproportionate likelihood of Black drivers being pulled over. His tweets come amid renewed national conversation on race and policing following high-profile deaths like Eric Garner and Michael Brown. While some social users advised him to "adapt" to avoid profiling, others criticized the expectation that Black individuals should change their behavior to prevent police stops.

Six people were injured in an explosion at a chemical plant in Fujian province, China, which sparked a large fire. The blast occurred at an oil storage facility after a leak, and the fire has been brought under control by over 600 firefighters. The plant, which produces a reportedly carcinogenic chemical, has a history of protests and previous explosions, having been relocated from a densely populated area due to pollution concerns.

The U.S. Department of Justice has charged FedEx with drug trafficking based on a 15-count indictment, arguing the courier service "constructively possessed" controlled substances shipped through its network. FedEx maintains its innocence, arguing that as a "common carrier" it cannot be held liable for the contents of packages it delivers, likening the situation to a mail carrier not knowing what is inside a letter. Mark Wahlberg is set to star in and produce "Patriots' Day," a film about Boston Police Commissioner Ed Davis and the manhight following the 2013 Boston Marathon bombing. The project, being produced by CBS Films, will be told from Davis' perspective and is the second major film announced regarding the tragedy, following Fox's "Boston Strong."

On Thursday's "The Price Is Right," model Manuela Arbelaez accidentally revealed the correct answer to a guessing game for a new Hyundai Sonata, causing host Drew Carey to laugh uncontably. Arbelaez was mortified by the slip, but she later tweeted that everything turned out OK. The incident occurred amid a busy week for the show, which saw former host Bob Barker, 91, make a surprise appearance on Wednesday.

Authorities identified Carlos Colina, 32, as the suspect in the discovery of human remains in a duffel bag in Cambridge, Massachusetts, over the weekend. Colina was arraigned on charges of assault, battery causing serious bodily injury, and improper disposal of a body, with the victim identified as 26-year-old Jonathan Camilien. Police believe the two knew each other, and the investigation remains ongoing as they await further medical examiner results to determine if additional charges are warranted.

"Arrested Development" is returning for a fifth season of 17 episodes, as confirmed by executive producer Brian Grazer. The news comes after a long hiatus following the show's cancellation by Fox and its move to Netflix for its fourth season. While it is not yet confirmed if the full cast will return, fans can expect more of the quirky comedy that the series is known for.

"Mad Men" returns Sunday for its final season, marking the end of an era for the acclaimed 1960s drama. The series, which has mirrored the disintegration of the 1960s through the lens of an advertising agency, will likely pick up immediately after the moon landing in July 1969, navigating the era's final turbulence including the Manson murders and the Vietnam War moratorium. Don Draper and his colleagues face an uncertain future as Sterling Cooper loses its founding partner and falls under the control of the Madison Avenue giant, McCann Erickson.

Nina Dobrev announced she will leave "The Vampire Diaries" after the current season, concluding her six-year run as Elena Gilbert. Fans expressed outrage and sadness over her departure, fearing it will prevent a satisfying resolution to the "Delena" romance. Producer Julie Plec confirmed the show will continue without Dobrev, focusing on the Salvatore brothers as it heads toward its May finale.

Federal education minister Smriti Irani discovered a security camera pointed at a changing room during a visit to a FabIndia store in Goa, leading to the arrest of four employees. Police allege the camera was capable of photographing customers, and the arrested staff face charges of voyeurism and breach of privacy, potentially facing up to three years in jail if convicted. FabIndia has condemned the incident and is cooperating with investigators as the manager remains at large.

Nine British citizens, including four children, were arrested in Turkey while attempting to cross illegally into Syria. The group, which included three men and two women, was detained at the Turkey-Syria border, and the British Foreign Office is currently seeking information from Turkish authorities regarding the incident.

A nuclear submarine undergoing repairs at the Zvyozdochka shipyard in Russia caught fire, reportedly starting during welding work. Authorities stated the vessel had been unloaded of nuclear fuel and armaments, and no injuries were reported. The incident is currently under investigation, with the shipyard's personnel evacuated as the fire was extinguished.

Turkish music icon Kayahan, 66, died of cancer on Friday, five days after his birthday. The singer, known for hits like "I Made a Vow," had first battled the disease in 1990 before it returned in 2005 and 2014. He is remembered as a defining voice in Turkish pop and folk music.

China's former top security czar, Zhou Yongkang, has been formally charged with accepting bribes, abuse of power, and leaking state secrets, making him the highest-ranking official ever to face corruption charges. The 72-year-old retired official, once a member of the powerful Politburo Standing Committee, was expelled from the Communist Party last December and his case will be tried in Tianjin. The article explores how Jesus and his disciples sustained themselves during their ministry, noting that while Jesus preached against the perils of wealth, the group relied on a common purse and likely survived through donations from supporters and hospitality from friends, functioning at a subsistence level.

Three people were killed and five others wounded after armed assailants stormed the attorney general's office in Balkh province, northern Afghanistan. Although most staff and civilians have been rescued, an exchange of fire between Afghan security forces and the attackers is ongoing, with security forces advancing cautiously to avoid civilian casualties. Two police officers and a security guard were among the dead.

Rand Paul's presidential campaign launch has drawn sharp criticism from Kentucky State Senator Georgia Bell, who argues his rhetoric on civil rights and voting rights is regressive and lacks substance, particularly given his opposition to the Civil Rights Act and voting protections while dismissively citing the presence of an African-American President as sufficient progress.

TV5Monde, a French-language global network, was hit by a "extremely powerful cyberattack" on Wednesday, causing its 11 channels and social media to go offline. The network reported it was hacked by an Islamist group, with ISIS logos appearing on its accounts, though no group claimed responsibility. By Thursday, the network had partially restored one channel and its Facebook page, though many website pages remained under maintenance.

Abu Dhabi-based Etihad Airways is investigating the disappearance of a 2-year-old cat named Felix, who went missing after arriving at New York's John F. Kennedy Airport on April 1. Jennifer Stewart and her husband had booked the cat for their job relocation from the UAE to the U.S., paying $1,200 for the 14-hour flight, but believe the cat escaped due to a damaged carrier. The airline, which shipped over 200 pets last year, has hired third-party specialists to search for the animal, calling the incident "extremely rare

Tuesday's headlines are dominated by high-stourt proceedings and political announcements. In Massachusetts, the trials of Aaron Hernandez and Dzhokhar Tsarnaev are nearing conclusions, with Hernandez's jury set to deliberate on circumstantial evidence and Tsarnaev facing a penalty phase on 30 charges related to the Boston Marathon bombing. Meanwhile, Senator Rand Paul officially launched his presidential campaign in Louisville, and Chicago voters face a surprising mayororal runoff between Rahm Emanuel and Jesus "Chuy" Garcia, all against the backdrop of ongoing tensions in Ferguson, Missouri.

A massive fire broke out Friday morning at a General Electric Appliance Park in Louisville, Kentucky, sending thick smoke over the area. Authorities reported no injuries or trapped individuals as they worked to contain the blaze, which had reached at least four alarms. The cause of the fire remains unknown, though the facility is described as a large complex capable of housing the equivalent of 34 football fields.

Cedar Falls, Iowa (CNN) -- Ted Cruz worked to energize Iowa's evangelical base during his first trip as a presidential candidate, connecting with voters through religious rhetoric and personal testimonies. Despite the commotion of the campaign trail, Cruz prioritized one-on-one interactions, emphasizing his brand as a stalwart conservative willing to champion social issues and religious liberty. With the state's vocal Christian right poised to decide the caucus, Cruz is positioning himself as the candidate to claim the coveted state as his prize.

Kenyans are mourning 147 victims, mostly students, killed in a terrorist attack at Garissa University College. Using the hashtag #147notjustanumber, citizens shared victims' stories and photos to honor their hopes and dreams that were cut down. The attack, claimed by the Somalia-based extremist group, is Kenya's deadliest since the 1998 U.S. Embassy bombing, with churches mourning the dead during Easter services.

The California Public Utilities Commission ordered Pacific Gas & Electric Co. to pay a record $1.6 billion penalty for unsafe gas transmission operations, following the 2010 San Bruno pipeline explosion that killed eight people. Most of the funds will be allocated to pipeline safety infrastructure improvements, with PG&E's CEO stating the company is dedicated to re-earning public trust and preventing future tragedies.

A Boston jury found Dzhokhar Tsarnaev guilty on all 30 counts, including 17 capital charges, making him eligible for the death penalty. The trial will now move into a penalty phase where jurors will weigh aggravating factors against mitigating ones to decide whether he will be executed. Despite the defense's admission that Tsarnaev was present at the bombing, his lawyer attempted to shift blame to his deceased brother, arguing he was merely following orders to persuade the jury to spare his life.

A massive fire broke off the coast of Mexico Wednesday, killing four workers and injuring 45 others at a Pemex oil platform. The blaze, which began in the dehydration and pumping area, was extinguished by night after a large-scale evacuation and response from at least 10 boats. Pemex denied rumors of a platform collapse and oil spills as the cause of the fire remained undetermined.

Easter is unique on the Christian calendar, a major point in the religious year that has resisted commercialization, and centers on Holy Week—the three-day period of Easter Triduum beginning with Good Friday's crucifixion, continuing through Holy Saturday, and culminating in Easter Sunday. Despite the cultural focus on identity and ethics, the holiday engenders a profound awareness of the human condition, calling those who approach it with seriousness of intent to explore its meaning.

Police in India are deploying pepper-spraying drones to manage violent crowds, with four already purchased and a fifth pending. The drones, fitted with cameras and spray mechanisms, have been tested successfully and will be used during protests or mob attacks, though their use has drawn mixed reactions regarding freedom of speech and the need for regulation. The initiative is set to be officially launched by the Chief Minister of Lucknow later this month.

A female employee accused Xavier Morales, a supervisor, of assault after he made sexual advances at her during a party at a brewery. The Secret Service has placed Morales on leave and suspended his security clearance following the March 31 incident, which Director Joe Clancy called "very disturbing." This scandal is the latest controversy for an agency already under scrutiny for multiple lapses, including a drone crash on the White House lawn and a fence jumper gaining access to the East Room.

Investigators have finished collecting evidence from the Germanwings crash site in the Alps, with the flight data and cockpit voice recorders recovered. Authorities report that the co-pilot, Andreas Lubitz, locked the captain out of the cockpit and used controls to speed up the plane's descent before crashing. All 150 people on board were killed, and officials say the site will remain secured until all debris is analyzed.
April 8 is celebrated as "Rex Manning Day" from the 1995 film *Empire Records*, while April 14 honors the romance of Jack and Rose from *Titanic*, and October 3 is recognized as "Mean Girls Day."

Twisted Sister has announced that their 2016 tour will be their final, marking the band's 40th anniversary with a farewell tour titled "Forty and F*ck It." Frontman Dee Snider confirmed the news, noting that the band will perform two shows in New Jersey and Las Vegas in memory of late drummer A.J. Pero.

"Grace of Monaco," starring Nicole Kidman, is heading straight to Lifetime after a tumultuous release path. The film, which premiered at last year's Cannes Film Festival, will air on the network on Memorial Day, May 25. Following poor international engagement, The Weinstein Co. decided to sell the rights directly to Lifetime rather than book it into U.S. theaters.

A massive tornado tore through Rochelle, Illinois, flattening homes and destroying a local restaurant, though no fatalities were reported. The storm cut a 22-mile path through Ogle County, causing significant damage and trapping some residents, but emergency responders confirmed that lives were spared despite the widespread destruction.

A bystander's cell phone video contradicted the initial police report, showing North Charleston Officer Michael Slager shooting Walter Scott eight times as he fled. Slager has been charged with murder after the footage revealed he planted an object near Scott's body and handcuffed him post-shooting. The incident began after Scott was pulled over for a broken taillight, with witnesses stating he did not grab the officer's Taser.

Kanye West has settled a civil lawsuit with paparazzi photographer Daniel Ramos, who he attacked at Los Angeles International Airport in 2013. The case was dismissed after West apologized to Ramos and reached an agreement, avoiding a trial that was set to begin next week. The settlement resolves the legal dispute stemming from the incident where West attempted to take Ramos' camera, resulting in a misdemeanor battery plea and probation for the rapper.

Don McLean's "American Pie" is a 44-year-old cultural touchstone that blends poetry, folk, and rock to memorialize the deaths of Buddy Holly, Ritchie Valens, and J.P. "The Big Bopper" Richardson. The song's original 16-page handwritten manuscript recently sold for $1.2 million at Christie's, underscoring its enduring status as an "essential Americana poem."

Mary Kay Letourneau Fualaau and her husband, Vili Fualaau, are celebrating their 10th wedding anniversary despite a relationship that began when she was a teacher and he was her 13-year-old student. Letourneau served over seven years in prison for charges related to their sexual relationship before the couple wed in 2005. In an upcoming "20/20" interview, she plans to have her sex offender status lifted while her husband discusses his struggles with alcoholism and depression.

Don McLean's original manuscript for "American Pie" sold for $1.2 million at Christie's, marking the third highest price for an American literary manuscript. The 16-page draft, filled with handwritten notes and deleted lyrics, offers a rare glimpse into the creation of the 1972 chart-topping epic. McLean, now 70, sold the work to support his family, noting he was motivated by a desire to "get the best deal" for his children and wife.

He shaved his head, trimmed his eyelashes, and used the nickname "JoJo" on his applications, receiving interview invitations at 11 schools before being accepted by St. Louis University. John Travolta has criticized HBO's documentary "Going Clear: Scientology and the Prison of Belief," calling it a result of "disgruntled" former members and defending Scientology as a positive force in his life, particularly crediting it with helping him cope with his son's death. He stated he hasn't seen the film and doesn't care to, arguing that his own positive experience contradicts the documentary's negative portrayal. Travolta, a high-profile Scientologist, is currently promoting his new film "The Forger" in Clearwater, Florida.

Anthony Ray Hinton was released from Alabama's death row after nearly 30 years, having been convicted of murders he says he didn't commit. The state dropped charges against him after new ballistics testing proved the gun he was accused of using could not match evidence in the cases. Hinton, who maintained his innocence throughout his imprisonment, expressed gratitude for his freedom while acknowledging the profound injustice of spending decades on death row for a crime he did not commit.

B.B. King was hospitalized for dehydration caused by his Type II diabetes but was released the same day after reassuring fans he was "much better." The 89-year-old blues legend, who was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1987, is resting at home and enjoying time with his grandchildren. He has postponed touring in the past due to similar health issues, but continues to perform for his devoted fanbase.

A giraffe at the Dallas Zoo gave birth to a calf early Friday evening after a highly publicized, hour-long labor streamed live on the Internet. The newborn, standing about 6 feet tall, was observed trying to nurse and moving its ears, marking a successful delivery after the mother's 15-month gestation. The zoo and fans celebrated the arrival of the calf, who joins a sister named Jamie.

The U.S. administration has abandoned plans for an Iraqi-led Mosul offensive this spring, citing no set timeline for the operation. While officials confirm ISIS has been degraded following the recapture of Tikrit, the fight for Mosul is deemed a complex endeavor requiring significant time and preparation, with no immediate ground assault planned despite ongoing airstrikes.

Season five of "Game of Thrones" premieres simultaneously in 170 countries, marking a major expansion for the series. Executive producers confirm that major story arcs are converging, with characters like Tyrion and Daenerys and the Night's Watch intersecting, while the narrative accelerates past the source material. The season teases escalating conflict as the common folk rise against noble warfare, setting up a crescendo toward the series' eventual conclusion.

A popular Chinese TV host, Bi Fujian, faced backlash after a video surfaced showing him cursing Chairman Mao Zedong during an impromptu performance. The clip, which went viral before being censored, sparked debate over free speech in China, with many criticizing Bi for violating taboos while others defended him as a private joke taken out of context.

A federal jury found Dzhokhar Tsarnaev guilty on all 30 counts related to the 2013 Boston Marathon bombings and their aftermath, delivering a mix of emotions for survivors like Rebekah Gregory, who testified about the attack's lasting trauma. While the verdict marks a significant step toward accountability, many victims emphasized that no sentence can fully heal the pain they endured, with some hoping to move forward while others debate whether Tsarnaev should face the death penalty. Richard Dysart, the Emmy-winning actor best known for portraying Leland McKenzie on "L.A. Law," has died at 86. His wife confirmed he passed away at home in Santa Monica after a long illness. Beyond his iconic TV role, Dysart had a prolific career spanning theater, film, and television, notably portraying historical figures like Harry Truman and J. Edgar Hoover.

The article argues that the current nuclear deal with Iran is dangerously weak, as it allows Tehran to maintain its nuclear infrastructure while receiving billions in sanctions relief. The author contends that President Obama is relinquishing critical U.S. leverage and that the agreement lacks the "anytime, anywhere" inspections necessary to prevent Iran from quickly developing a bomb. Furthermore, the deal is criticized for potentially empowering Iran's regional proxies and failing to impose verifiable, long-term constraints on its nuclear program.

The VII Summit of the Americas in Panama City devolved into a "triangle of tension" between the U.S., Cuba, and Venezuela. While President Obama and Cuban President Raul Castro were poised for a historic handshake following the 2014 detente, Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro escalated tensions by banning U.S officials and rallying allies like Cuba, which publicly condemned new U.S sanctions. The summit was further complicated by Maduro's efforts to mobilize regional support against American policies, overshadowing the anticipated U.S.-Cuba détente.

Former Maryland Governor Martin O'Malley and former Senator Jim Webb, both Democratic presidential hopefuls, shared a stage in Des Moines, Iowa, but remain ideologically distant. O'Malley engaged enthusiastically with supporters, while Webb maintained a low-profile, stoic demeanor. Both face long odds against the frontrunner, Hillary Clinton, polling at minimal support compared to her dominant standing in the race.

The Taliban released a biography of Mullah Mohammed Omar to dispel rumors of his death and affirm his leadership of the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan. The 11-page document details his daily routine and early life, aiming to counter speculation that the reclusive founder has died. The publication comes as ISIS leader Abu Bakr al-B Baghdadi has declared himself caliph, highlighting the Taliban's leadership challenges.

A viral photo of a cat on stairs has sparked a debate over whether the feline is ascending or descending, drawing comparisons to the viral "The Dress" illusion. The image, shared on Imgur and 9gag.com, has captivated internet users who are divided by their perception of the cat's motion and the stairs' design. Advertisers have quickly jumped in to capitalize on the trending discussion.

Tornado sirens sounded across Kansas and Missouri Wednesday night as severe storms produced multiple twisters, including one reported near Goddard and others near Aetna. The system also brought reports of large hail and flooding, with the National Weather Service warning that nighttime tornadoes are particularly dangerous. Additional storms are expected across the Midwest and South on Thursday.

After his brother's death, a lifelong Catholic stopped praying and left the Church, feeling shut out by parish rules. Years later, Pope Francis’s emphasis on compassion and "inner freedom" reawakened his faith, particularly through the Cardinal's explanation that the Pope’s non-judgmental tone—like "If a person is gay and he searches for the Lord and has good will, who am I to judge?"—mirrors Christ’s love rather than condemnation.

Liana Barrientos, 39, is facing criminal charges for allegedly falsely claiming on a 2010 marriage license application that it was her "first and only" marriage, despite having been married 10 times between 1999 and 2002. Prosecutors allege the marriages were part of an immigration scam, with several husbands filing for permanent residence, and she was arrested after pleading not guilty for subway trespass. If convicted, she faces up to four years in prison.

Washington was rocked by a series of connected shootings that began with a domestic kidnapping. The suspect fled the scene, leading police on a chase that ended in a crash on H Street, where an officer and the suspect were both wounded. Authorities believe the suspect kidnapped a victim before opening fire at the U.S. Census Bureau and a nearby restaurant district, with the guard and kidnap victim both located and in good condition.

Amnesty International's report "Their Lives on the Line" highlights the escalating persecution of women's rights activists in Afghanistan, documenting attacks by the Taliban, tribal warlords, and government officials. The report underscores the dangerous environment following Farkhunda's murder, noting that women activists face lethal risks with little protection, as perpetrators often act free and authorities frequently ignore reported threats. Despite this lethal climate, activists continue their work with remarkable resilience, persistently demanding accountability and women's rights.

The University of Michigan initially canceled a screening of "American Sniper" after student objections, but reversed the decision following backprint, allowing the film to proceed while offering "Paddington" as an alternative. Vice President E. Royster Harper stated the cancellation was a mistake, emphasizing the university's commitment to free expression and student choice. The reversal was praised by head football coach Jim Harbaugh.

An Indian court sentenced software pioneer Ramalinga Raju and nine others to seven years in prison for orchestrating a massive $1.6 billion fraud at Satyam Computers Services. The scandal, dubbed India's biggest corporate fraud, involved inflating profits with fictitious assets and led to the company's board being dissolved and sold to Tech Mahindra. Raju, 60, who founded the company in 1987, has been in jail for the past 32 months.

A 32-year-old man, Carlos Colina, has been charged with murder in connection with the discovery of a 26-year-old man's remains in a duffel bag in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Police linked Colina to the crime through surveillance footage after the remains were found near the police department headquarters. The suspect was already out on bail for an unrelated assault case when he was arraigned on the murder charge on April 14.

"Star Wars" fans can purchase the first six films in digital HD starting Friday, with the release including exclusive behind-the-scenes features, such as sound designer Ben Burtt revealing how real animals were used to create the alien sounds for the Geonosians. The collection marks the first time the saga is available for digital download and introduces the franchise's first gay character.

An Iranian military observation aircraft flew dangerously close to a U.S. Navy helicopter over the Persian Gulf, sparking U.S. concerns that local Iranian commanders may not be in full control of their forces. The incident occurred as the U.S. and Iran negotiate a nuclear deal in Switzerland, and the U.S. is considering a formal protest, viewing the maneuver as potentially "locally ordered" and reprimanded by higher-ups.

Swedish photographer Johan Bavman documented fathers utilizing the country's generous 480-day parental leave policy, highlighting how the mandated "daddy months" promote bonding and challenge traditional gender roles. While only 12% of couples equally share leave, Bavman's project captures the physical and emotional realities of stay-at-home dads, aiming to normalize their often-t overlooked labor. He seeks to photograph 60 fathers to culminate in an exhibition and book, having currently found 35 willing subjects.

A judge ruled that Craig Hicks can face the death penalty for the deaths of three Muslim students in Chapel Hill, North Carolina. The victims—Yusor Mohammad, her husband Deah Shaddy Barakat, and her sister Razan Mohammad Abu-Salha—were shot in the head during an ongoing neighbor dispute over parking. Authorities are also investigating the shootings as a possible hate crime, alongside a parallel federal inquiry.

HBO released a teaser for "True Detective" Season 2, premiering June 21. The season follows four protagonists—a compromised detective, a criminal entrepreneur, a sheriff's detective, and a war veteran—as they navigate a web of conspiracy and betrayal in California. The first season, starring Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson, was a hit that famously crashed the HBO Go site during its finale.

Lauren Hill, the 19-year-old Indiana woman who inspired the nation by playing college basketball while battling brain cancer, passed away early Friday. Her story captivated the world last year when Mount St. Joseph University accelerated its season opener to fulfill her dream, and she ultimately used her platform to raise $1.4 million for pediatric cancer research. Hill's death was mourned by coaches, teammates, and public figures like LeBron James, who hailed her as the "true definition of strength and courage."

Chris Copeland of the Indiana Pacers was stabbed outside a New York nightclub early Wednesday. Two Atlanta Hawks players, Pero Antic and Thabo Sefolosha, were arrested on obstruction and disorderly conduct charges after going to check on their friend; they were not involved in the stabbing. The suspect fled the scene but was later taken into custody, and Copeland and his companion were hospitalized.

While acknowledging Clinton as "eminently qualified," O'Malley suggested lesser-known candidates can rise if they make their case to voters, and reiterated that a robust primary with multiple contenders would be better for the party. Hip-hop star Nelly was arrested in Tennessee on drug and weapon charges after a state trooper pulled over his tour bus for missing registration stickers. During the search, police found methamphetamine, marijuana, drug paraphernalia, and multiple handguns, including a gold-plated .50-caliber pistol. Nelly and another passenger were taken to jail, where the rapper posted bond before being released.

Hundreds gathered in Summerville to celebrate the life of Walter Scott, a U.S. Coast Guard veteran fatally shot by a police officer, as a catalyst for change in America. The funeral service, attended by local officials and mourners, highlighted the racial prejudice surrounding Scott's death and called for justice, with his family emphasizing that his death would not be in vain. Following the service, Scott was privately buried at Live Oak Memorial Gardens, while his family's attorney emphasized the case as a broader human issue regarding police accountability.

For 12 years, Adelma Cifuentes endured severe abuse from her husband in rural Guatemala, culminating in a near-fatal attack where she lost her arm. Despite Guatemala's alarmingly high femicide rate—where nearly 10 women are killed per 100,000 and two are killed daily—98% of cases never reach court due to entrenched gender bias, impunity from the civil war, and lack of resources. Hillary Clinton officially launched her 2016 presidential campaign, leveraging her extensive political experience and name recognition to position herself as a strong Democratic contender. However, to avoid past mistakes and the scrutiny of her authenticity, she must articulate a compelling vision for the White House rather than relying on the perception of inevitability. The success of her run will depend on her ability to connect with voters directly and navigate Republican attacks without appearing stiff or inauthentic.

"Lost River," Ryan Gosling's directorial debut, premiered at Cannes to polarized reception but has found renewed appreciation as a theatrical release. Set against the decaying backdrop of Detroit, the film uses the city's crumbling infrastructure as both a literal and metaphorical engine for its narrative about displaced communities and urban ruin. While Gosling frames the project as a visceral exploration of "Lost Rivers"—neighborhoods erased by demolition and neglect—the film ultimately finds humanity in the salvage of copper piping and artistic regeneration amidst the devastation.

7-Eleven is hosting its first "Bring-Your-Own-Cup Slurpee Day" on Saturday, allowing customers to fill their own containers for $1.49 at participating stores. The promotion runs from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. and is designed to kick off peak Slurpee season, though participants must adhere to size and sanitation rules. The event is distinct from the traditional Free Slurpee Day celebrated every July 11.

Elizabeth Sedway was removed from an Alaska Airlines flight in Hawaii after stating she had cancer and lacked a doctor's note. Despite eventually flying home, she missed chemotherapy and important family commitments, and the airline apologized for the disruption and refunded her tickets.

Rolling Stone retracted a 2014 article about an alleged gang rape at the University of Virginia, but the incident highlighted a broader issue: the university has never expelled a student for sexual assault despite a pattern of mishaging such cases. Following the retraction, multiple women came forward to describe a campus culture that minimized or ignored sexual assault, prompting the Virginia attorney general to investigate how UVA historically handled these allegations.

The Department of Justice will begin negotiations to restructure the Ferguson Police Department following a report documenting a pattern of racial discrimination and excessive force. The review was prompted by the killing of Michael Brown and subsequent protests, which led to the election of two new Black city council members and the resignation of the town manager. Ultimately, the DOJ report revealed that the police department functioned as "a collection agency" that preyed disproportionately on African-American residents through illegal stops and excessive force.

A 36-year-old passenger died after a Lamborghini crashed into a guardrail at the Exotic Driving Experience at Walt Disney World Speedway on Sunday. The 24-year-old driver lost control of the vehicle and was hospitalized with minor injuries. Petty Holdings, which operates the attraction, released a statement extending sympathies to those involved in the tragic accident.

A passenger on an Atlanta-bound Air Canada flight attempted to choke Ottawa Fury forward Oliver Minatel with a cord during the flight from Toronto. Fellow passengers and crew intervened to restrain the suspect, who was later evaluated by authorities mid-flight. The plane landed safely in Atlanta, where the man was escorted off by U.S. officials, allowing Minatel to remain uninjured and ready for his team's upcoming match.

A federal grand jury has charged Robert Durst, a convicted felon and real estate heir, with unlawful possession of a firearm. Authorities allege he possessed a .38 caliber revolver found in his hotel room last month, adding to a litany of accusations including the first-degree murder charge related to the death of Susan Berman. Durst, who is currently held without bail and awaiting extradition to Los Angeles, faces significant prison time and potentially the death penalty if convicted.

A photographer has discovered over 1,800 pieces of graffiti in an underground city in France, left by World War I soldiers. The site, which dates back centuries and was sealed until the 18th century, was recently reopened after a consortium of villages purchased the rights to promote its historical awareness. The inscriptions, which range from Australian and British soldiers to 55 Americans, provide a human connection to the men who lived and died a century ago.

President Obama's nomination of Loretta Lynch to become the first African-American woman attorney general has become a historic wait, as her confirmation vote by the full Senate has dragged into a record-breaking sixth month. The delay, which has lasted longer for Lynch than any recent nominee, has drawn criticism from civil rights advocates who suggest race is a major factor in the holdup, while supporters in Durham, North Carolina, celebrate her as a hometown daughter.

Scientists are optimistic about finding life beyond Earth within the next decade or two, noting that the discovery of thousands of exoplanets—including many Earth-like, habitable-zone worlds—suggests that simple life may be common. However, the emergence of intelligent, communicative civilizations is considered highly unlikely, as human-like technology has only existed on Earth for a tiny fraction of the planet's history. While the sheer number of potential Earth-like planets improves the odds, the chances of discovering life that can communicate via radio waves remain astronomically low due to vast temporal and evolutionary gaps.

Prosecutors spent months presenting 131 witnesses to establish Aaron Hernandez's guilt in the death of Odin Lloyd, while the defense wrapped up its case in less than a day. With the jury now poised to deliberate, much of the evidence remains circumstantial, particularly centring on Hernandez's inconsistent alibi and the mysterious contents of a box his fiancée was asked to dispose of. Key points for the jury to consider include the discrepancy in Robert Kraft's testimony regarding the timing of Lloyd's death and the contested forensic details surrounding the shoes and the unrecovered murder weapon.

At the 2015 Masters, Jordan Spieth maintained his dominant lead entering the final round, finishing twelve under par to take a four-shot advantage over Justin Rose. Despite late challenges from Tiger Woods and Phil Mickelson, Spieth's composence under pressure secured him a five-shot lead heading into Sunday, putting him on track for his second major title.

A Delaware family fell ill during a trip to the U.S. Virgin Islands, likely due to pesticide exposure at their rental villa. The father is stable but improving, while his two sons remain in critical condition; the mother has been treated and released. Officials suspect methyl bromide, a restricted and toxic chemical, caused the sickness after a possible fumigation at the resort.

A New York judge recently authorized the service of divorce papers via Facebook, highlighting the evolving nature of "service of process." While traditional in-person service is the gold standard, courts have increasingly allowed alternative methods—such as social media—when defendants evade traditional notice. This ruling underscores that while "traditional" service methods aren't always "good," the use of Facebook is viewed as a last-resort solution to ensure a defendant is notified of a lawsuit.

The UNRWA commissioner-general is visiting Yarmouk camp to assess the worsening humanitarian crisis affecting 18,000 civilians, including 3,500 children. The camp, largely controlled by armed groups and cut off from aid since late 2013, has seen severe shortages of medical care and reports of malnutrition. Krähenbühl aims to meet with local and international officials to relieve the suffering of those trapped in the conflict-stricken area.

A daring raid on a London jewelry district safe deposit box facility over the Easter weekend resembles a heist movie like "Ocean 11," marking one of the few "old-style" burglaries in the city in over 40 years. Unlike modern cybercrime, the gang relied on physical planning and inside information to execute the burglary. While such sophisticated heists are rare and typically motivated by funding criminal enterprises or a certain lifestyle rather than challenge, they require a specific blend of high intellect and street-level intelligence to convert stolen goods into untraceable cash.

Fans of Paul Walker were moved to tears by the emotional tribute in "Furious 7," which opened with a record $146 million debut. The filmmakers used body doubles and CGI to complete Walker's scenes, ultimately choosing to retire his character Brian in a sincere send-off rather than killing him off. The montage set to "See You Again" served as a heartfelt farewell, leaving audiences choked up but praising the fitting homage.

Selena's family is launching a hologram-like digital embodiment of the late singer to preserve her legacy and engage new fans. The "Selena the One" project, developed by Nevada-based Acrovirt LLC, will feature the singer autonomously learning and reacting, with plans for new music and a potential 2018 tour. The initiative aims to celebrate Selena's enduring popularity through technology rather than replace her, with fans able to support the launch via an Indiegogo campaign starting April 16.

A gastrointestinal illness outbreak has affected over 100 people on the Celebrity Infinity, with 95 passengers and five crew members reporting symptoms such as vomiting and diarrhea. The CDC is currently investigating the cause of the ailment as the ship prepares to dock in San Diego. This marks the third such outbreak for the vessel since 2006.

The original cast of Twin Peaks has rallied behind David Lynch, launching a #SaveTwinPeaks campaign to prevent his exit over a salary dispute. The actors argue that reviving the series without Lynch is "like pies without cherries," emphasizing his essential creative role. Despite the protest, Showtime has renewed other series like Shameless and Happyish while Lynch announced his departure, though the network hopes to reach a resolution to keep the creators on board.

A former TSA agent was sentenced to six months in jail and five and a half years of probation for secretly videotaping a female co-worker in a bathroom and entering her home to steal data. The investigation revealed over 90 videos and 1,500 photos of the victim on the defendant's devices. The judge called the invasion of privacy "egregious," noting the breach of trust and digital privacy.

Five Chinese feminists face up to five years in prison for planning International Women's Day events, with charges recently changed from "picking quarrels" to "assembling a crowd to disturb public order." Amnesty International and legal advocates argue the women were simply advocating for gender equality and legal protections, while the detention has drawn international condemnation from figures like Hillary Clinton and human rights groups.

A fiberglass boat fragment from the 2011 Japan tsunami was spotted off the Oregon coast and towed to Newport, where biologists discovered yellowtail jack fish—normally native to Japanese waters—living inside. While the ecological threat was deemed small, the debris will be taken to a landfill, but the fish will be relocated to the Oregon Coast Aquarium.

Two Alabama college students, Ryan Calhoun and Delonte Martistee, have been arrested and charged with sexual battery following a gang rape that occurred during spring break in Panama City Beach, Florida. The investigation was initiated after Troy University police discovered video evidence of the assault, which took place behind the Spinnaker Beach Club between March 10 and March 12, 2015. Both suspects have been suspended by the university and face their first court appearance Saturday, with the Bay County Sheriff's Office indicating that further arrests are expected.

The refinery, located just outside Tikrit, is a key strategic target, and if damaged, it could significantly impact Iraq's domestic fuel supply.

A contractor fell asleep in the pressurized and temperature-controlled cargo hold of an Alaska Airlines flight traveling from Seattle to Los Angeles. After hearing bumping and screams from below, the pilot turned back mid-air, and a federal air marshal helped guide an emergency landing. The worker was hospitalized but later discharged after passing a drug test.

One year after the abduction of nearly 300 schoolgirls by Boko Haram in Chibok, Nigeria, the tragedy continues to haunt the families and the world, with many still missing and a global outcry demanding their return. While the incoming president has pledged an aggressive crackdown on the militants, the group still controls vast territories in the northeast, and over 800,000 children remain displaced by the ongoing conflict.

A hooded angel with black wings appeared near the site where Walter Scott was shot and killed, becoming an icon for the Black Lives Matter movement. Artist Phillip Hyman created the artwork to mourn Scott's death and allow the family to grieve, prefering viewers to interpret the piece themselves. The artwork has been used in protests outside North Charleston's City Hall, with Hyman happy to let it "do what it's supposed to do."

After his tech startup failed to secure investment, Jia Jiang launched the "100 Days of Rejection" project to confront his fear of rejection. Through increasingly bold public requests—ranging from asking a Krispy Kreme manager to make Olympic-themed donuts to seeking investment from strangers—Jiang documented his journey in the best-selling book "Rejection Proof," aiming to reframe rejection as an opportunity for growth rather than a reason to quit.

CNN correspondents witnessed a scene from "Make Way for Ducklings" on a rainy Washington street, where they stopped traffic to help a mother duck and her brood safely cross L Street NW. The bystanders, including a man who surrendered his umbrella, guided the family to a grassy area at 16th and L streets, an event the reporters called "an extraordinary situation" given the rarity of such wildlife encounters in the city center.

Police added attempted murder charges to a mother accused of leaving her quadriplegic son in a Philadelphia park for days. Nyia Parler cannot be extruded to face the charges until she completes an unspecified treatment in Maryland. Once extradited, she will face additional counts of aggravated assault, reckless endangerment, and related offenses.

A U.S. RC-135U reconnaissance plane was intercepted by a Russian SU-27 Flanker over the Baltic Sea in international airspace, with the U.S. condemining the Russian pilot's "unsafe and unprofessional" maneuvers. The Pentagon and State Department are filing a diplomatic petition regarding the incident, which marks the latest in a series of similar encounters between Russian and U.S. aircraft.

His mother, Nyia Parler, was taken into custody in Maryland but cannot be extruded to face charges until she completes an unspecified medical treatment. Officials report the man is in stable condition and recovering in the hospital.

Kansas has enacted the first U.S. law banning "dismemberment" abortion procedures, which are commonly used during the second trimester. The law, signed by Governor Sam Brownback, allows the procedure only to protect the mother's life or health, but opponents argue it severely restricts access and endangers women's health. Both sides anticipate legal challenges, with supporters viewing it as a groundbreaking step toward protecting fetal life.

Jill Dillard, the first daughter from "19 Kids and Counting," gave birth to a son named Israel David on Monday. The baby arrived over a week past his due date, and Jill, a student midwife, had mentally prepared for the wait. Her parents, Jim Bob and Michelle Duggar, shared the news on their Facebook page, marking her as the first from the family to become a mother.

A former work-study student, Kenneth Morgan Stancil III, shot and killed longtime employee Ron Lane at Wayne Community College in Goldsboro, North Carolina. Authorities are investigating the incident as a possible hate crime, noting Lane was white and gay while the suspect has tattoos and is being investigated for possible white supremacist gang ties. Stancil fled the scene but was later arrested near 550 miles away after being found sleeping on a beach with a knife.

Former Australia cricket captain and legendary broadcaster Richie Benaud has died at the age of 84. A revered figure in the sport, he was celebrated for his record-breaking leg-spin bowling, his charimatic commentary, and his role in popularizing cricket globally, particularly through his long tenure with the BBC.

Irish betting company Paddy Power deleted a controversial tweet comparing Newcastle's 20-year losing streak to police brutality against unarmed Black men, issuing an apology that it was "me meant." The tweet, a play on Liverpool's "K Kop" end, was part of a statistical graphic ahead of their Premier League match, which Liverpool won 2-0. The incident drew widespread condemnation on social media, with critics calling for the tweet's author to be fired, joining a string of previous publicity stunts that have regularly landed the company in headlines.

Over 978 migrants were rescued in the Mediterranean on Friday, part of a larger influx where more than 10,000 have arrived in Italy in just three months. The migrants, primarily from West Africa, Somalia, and Syria, are fleeing transit through Libya, but at least 480 have died attempting the crossing this year alone.

President Barack Obama reiterated his commitment to maintaining Israel's military advantage over Iran, stating he is willing to make security guarantees to ensure regional stability. He argued that the nuclear deal, which limits Iran's centrifuges and uranium enrichment in exchange for sanctions relief, is necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon, even if trust is lacking. Cape Verde, a nation of 500,000 people, leverages its rich musical heritage to drive economic development, positioning music as its primary national resource alongside fishing. While the government and international platforms acknowledge the sector's potential, a 2013 UN report noted the creative economy remains small with room for growth, though events like the Kriol Jazz Festival signal promising early success.

Kenya has frozen 86 bank accounts linked to suspected Al-Shabaab supporters following the Garissa university attack that killed 147 people. The government is tracking the finances of the militant group, which claimed responsibility for the massacre, and has been doing so since 2011. Additionally, Kenya launched airstrikes in Somalia targeting Al-Shabaab training camps and offered a reward for information on the attack's alleged organizer.

Jodi Arias was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole for the 2008 murder of Travis Alexander, after a jury failed to reach a unanimous decision on the death penalty. Maricopa County Judge Sherry Stephens opted for a life sentence over the chance of early release, citing the brutal nature of the crime and Arias' remorse. Chinese authorities have formally detained five women's rights activists, including Wu Rongrong, for planning to protest on International Women's Day against sexual harassment. The women face a legal deadline of April 13 to either be released or formally arrested, which rights groups say almost always leads to conviction. The detions come amid a year in which China is expected to adopt its first anti-domestic violence law and mark the 20th anniversary of a major women's rights conference.

Last week, Malala Yousafzai made history by becoming the first person to have an asteroid named in her honor while in outer space. NASA astrophysicist Amy Mainzer named the celestial body "316201 Malala" to recognize the activist's contributions to girls' education, noting that very few asteroids are named after women. The asteroid, which orbits between Mars and Jupiter, serves as a symbolic tribute to Malala's global impact.

Emy Afalava, born in American Samoa, is suing for citizenship despite being born on U.S. soil, arguing the Fourteenth Amendment guarantees his rights. The article traces a century-long legal battle, from the racist Dred Scott decision to the 1904 Isabel Gonzalez case, showing how the Supreme Court has historically denied citizenship to island-born residents while gradually expanding rights. A current lawsuit seeks to right this "injust," arguing that the Constitution's birthright citizenship principle, established since the nation's founding, should apply colorblindly to all U.S. territories.

Over the past year, more than 25,000 people contracted Ebola, with over 10,000 fatalities, making it the most severe public health emergency in modern history. While the epidemic's intensity has decreased and initial dire predictions have not materialized, dozens of new infections are still reported weekly. The World Health Organization reports indicate that while surveillance is improving and cases are falling in some regions, unknown chains of transmission continue to pose a risk of new infections.
